analysis.one_liner: Lets doctors build and expand physician-owned hospitals and bill Medicare for patients they refer there.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 2025 with 12 cosponsors, the bill was sent to two House committees, and no committee action or vote has taken place since.
analysis.plain_summary: Since the 2010 health law, doctors have been barred from building new hospitals they own, and existing physician-owned hospitals have been blocked from expanding, unless they gave up Medicare patients. This bill wipes out those limits and restores the pre-2010 rules. The stated goal is more patient access and quality, but the practical effect is that physicians with ownership stakes can again profit when they send their own patients to facilities they own and Medicare pays the bill.
analysis.who_benefits: Physicians who own or want to own hospitals. Repealing the limits lets them build new physician-owned hospitals or expand existing ones and keep their Medicare revenue, and it restores the ability to profit from self-referral — sending a patient they treat to a hospital they part-own.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Affordable Care Act sections (6001 and 10601) and the 2010 reconciliation act section (1106) that restrict, for Medicare purposes, self-referrals to newly built or expanded physician-owned hospitals [S2] [S3].
Restores the law as if those limits had never been enacted, so physician-owners could add beds, operating rooms, and new facilities and keep treating Medicare patients there [S3].
Sponsors frame this as opening patient access to higher-quality care, on the argument that physician-owned specialty hospitals compete and perform well on some measures.

analysis.who_pays: Community hospitals, which lose their most profitable surgical patients to physician-owned facilities while still absorbing emergency and charity care, and Medicare, which pays for services generated by self-referral; the added utilization flows to taxpayers and beneficiaries.

drawbacks.text: The core mechanism is self-referral: a doctor who owns part of a hospital earns money when that hospital treats the doctor's patients, a financial conflict of interest that exists whether or not the referral is medically needed.

Federal advisory analyses of physician-owned hospitals have found they tend to draw the most profitable patients and procedures, which raises Medicare spending and leaves community hospitals with the costlier caseload.
The changes only apply to Medicare participation; physicians could build facilities that serve Medicare patients, so the ACA-era constraint on growth is the specific thing being removed [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real but narrow: some patients gain access to specialty surgical hospitals, and physician-owned facilities have shown competitive quality and prices on certain procedures. The downside is structural: self-referral gives doctors a direct financial stake in their own treatment decisions, past federal reviews have found higher utilization and profitable-patient selection, and the bill is titled around patient access while its operative section is simply a repeal of the ownership limits. On balance it is an industry-backed rollback, not a patient-protection bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees the day it was introduced, and neither committee has taken it up, so no vote has been scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Beth Van Duyne introduced the bill on June 12, 2025, with nine original cosponsors; it picked up three more, reaching 12 cosponsors — 11 Republicans and 1 Democrat [S1] [S4] [S5].
The same day, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, with the Speaker to decide later which committee handles which provisions [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, floor vote, or Senate companion activity — appears in the action history after the referral [S5].

The bill's entire operative section is a repeal of ACA sections 6001 and 10601 and reconciliation-act section 1106, the provisions limiting Medicare participation for new or expanded physician-owned hospitals [S2] [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one yet, because nothing has happened: the bill has sat in committee since June 2025. If it stays there, community hospitals and the Medicare program are spared the utilization and cost effects, while physician-owners forgo the chance to expand.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No winner yet; bill sits in committee

for.name: Physician Hospitals of America
for.what_they_did: Longstanding advocate for repealing the ACA limits on physician-owned hospital expansion; backs identical measures in successive Congresses

against.name: American Hospital Association
against.role: Trade association for community and health-system hospitals
against.what_they_did: Has historically opposed loosening physician self-referral limits, arguing physician-owned hospitals siphon profitable patients from full-service community hospitals

sides.party_line_note: All 12 cosponsors signed on with no committee or floor vote yet: 11 Republicans and 1 Democrat (Rep. Cuellar of Texas).

industries.note: Repeal removes the ACA-era caps so they can build new or expanded facilities and keep Medicare revenue for patients they refer to hospitals they part-own. Their gain comes through self-referral, which ties their income to the volume of care they personally order.

Physician-owned specialty facilities draw the most profitable surgeries and diagnostics, leaving community hospitals with emergency, charity, and complex care while their profitable caseload shrinks. This erodes the cross-subsidy that funds care for everyone else.

More physician-owned capacity means more Medicare claims generated by self-referral, which federal reviews have tied to higher spending; patients may also get faster access to some specialty procedures. The cost and access effects pull in different directions.

analysis.trajectory: With no hearing or markup scheduled in either referral committee, the bill is following the pattern of earlier versions of this same measure, which have repeatedly been introduced and left in committee. Absent a push from committee leadership, it is likely to sit untouched for the rest of the session.
